episode_title: Commercial Insurance Coverage and Policy Stacks

segment_1.topic_phrase: how much insurance is actually behind the vehicle that hit you
segment_1.setup: I'm **{{INTERVIEWER}}**. Today is about something most people in Florida never think about until it matters. How much insurance is behind the vehicle that hits you, and why that number decides almost everything.
segment_1.credential: **{{ATTORNEY}}**, you've been taking these cases apart for **{{YEARS_PRACTICING}}** years.
segment_1.prompt: Somebody is still in a hospital gown and the insurance company is already building its side. Explain what they're doing in those first days. And if you've watched it play out on a case, take us through it.

attributes.name: Cases you took to trial
attributes.detail: The ones you put in front of a jury instead of settling, and how the insurers stacked above the first one behave once they believe you'll do it again.

attributes.name: Business vehicle crashes
attributes.detail: Not injury cases generally. Crashes caused by a commercial vehicle, how many, and how recently.

attributes.name: Credentials anyone can verify
attributes.detail: Your license and your disciplinary record, which matter more than any directory badge.

attributes.name: Who the carriers hire here
attributes.detail: The county court, the judges, and the defense firms the insurers around here actually retain.

attributes.name: Finding every policy
attributes.detail: How you get to the coverage nobody volunteers, including the layers stacked above the first one.

attributes.name: Reading the front page of the policy
attributes.detail: The one-page summary that lists the limits, and what on it decides whether a second and third policy can be reached at all.

attributes.name: Getting the limits in writing
attributes.detail: How you make an insurer state its number on paper, and why a number somebody gives you over the phone is worth nothing.

attributes.name: Putting a number on the future
attributes.detail: The experts who figure out what a lifetime of care actually costs, because that total is what you hold the insurance layers up against.

attributes.name: Evidence that gets erased
attributes.detail: What you lock down in the first days, before the vehicle data and the company records are overwritten.

attributes.name: Three separate clocks
attributes.detail: The medical window, the filing deadline, and the much shorter one if a public vehicle was involved.

attributes.name: Fees and who pays the costs
attributes.detail: What the percentage is, whether it goes up if you file suit, who fronts the cost of chasing every policy, and what happens if you lose.

attributes.name: When the money isn't there
attributes.detail: How you tell somebody the coverage doesn't exist, and why you say it in the first conversation instead of the tenth.

questions.q: Why does the insurance behind the other vehicle matter so much after a crash in Stuart?

bullets.label: A business vehicle isn't a car
bullets.detail: the policy behind it's usually many times the size of anything a private driver carries.

bullets.label: The coverage decides what's possible
bullets.detail: the injury sets what the case is worth, but the insurance behind it sets what you can actually collect.

bullets.label: Around here specifically
bullets.detail: most of the heavy traffic on I-95 and the Turnpike is freight passing through, so the vehicle that hit you often belongs to a company with far deeper coverage than anyone local.

questions.q: How is a commercial policy different from the car insurance most people have?

bullets.label: It's written for a business
bullets.detail: it covers the vehicle, the driver, and the company running both of them.

bullets.label: The numbers aren't comparable
bullets.detail: a personal policy is written in thousands and a commercial one is often written in millions.

bullets.label: There's usually more than one
bullets.detail: a business tends to carry layers, and the first policy anybody finds is rarely the only one.

bullets.label: What that looks like here
bullets.detail: a long-haul trucking company running the coast is insured as an interstate operation, and that policy is far bigger and far better documented than the one on a local van.

questions.q: What are policy limits, and why are they the number that matters most?

bullets.label: A policy limit's a ceiling
bullets.detail: no matter how badly somebody is hurt, that policy won't pay a dollar past it.

bullets.label: It sets the whole strategy
bullets.detail: that number decides how the case gets built and who else gets pulled into it.

bullets.label: Getting the number in writing
bullets.detail: Florida law lets us force the insurer to tell us the limit, and it has to come in writing so nobody can walk it back later.

questions.q: What kinds of commercial policies turn up in a crash in Stuart or across the Treasure Coast?

bullets.label: It depends on what was on the road
bullets.detail: on I-95 and the Turnpike it's long-haul freight, and on US 1 and Kanner Highway it's delivery vans and service trucks, and those are different policies entirely.

bullets.label: The business itself carries more
bullets.detail: there's often a separate policy covering the company's operations, not just the vehicle.

bullets.label: Who's named on it matters
bullets.detail: a contractor driving for a larger company may be covered by both, or by neither, and that's a document question.

questions.q: What does it actually mean to stack coverage?

bullets.label: Think of it as floors
bullets.detail: the first policy pays to its limit, then the next one starts, then the one above that.

bullets.label: Every floor is a separate fight
bullets.detail: each insurer above the first one has its own lawyers and its own reasons why the claim isn't its problem yet.

bullets.label: The total is what matters
bullets.detail: the number worth knowing is all of those layers added together, not what the first policy says.

questions.q: What's the difference between an umbrella policy and an excess policy?

bullets.label: Both sit on top
bullets.detail: neither one pays until the policy underneath it has been used up.

bullets.label: An excess policy copies the one below it
bullets.detail: same terms, same list of things it won't cover, just a higher ceiling.

bullets.label: Umbrella can be broader
bullets.detail: it sometimes covers things the policy underneath never did, which is why the wording gets read line by line.

questions.q: Can you stack insurance policies in Florida?

bullets.label: Sometimes, and it's worth checking
bullets.detail: more than one policy can be added together, and that's often where the real money is.

bullets.label: A form may have signed it away
bullets.detail: there's a form people sign that trades away stacking for a cheaper premium, and most of them never realize they signed it.

bullets.label: Go read it
bullets.detail: the one-page summary at the front of the policy from the year of the crash settles the argument, not what anyone remembers choosing.

questions.q: What happens when the vehicle that hit you in Stuart doesn't have enough coverage?

bullets.label: Your own policy can step in
bullets.detail: the coverage on your own car pays when the other side runs out or never had any.

bullets.label: It'sn't automatic
bullets.detail: it has to be claimed, and your own insurer will treat it like any other claim.

bullets.label: Then look wider
bullets.detail: a household policy, an employer's policy, and with the number of out-of-state drivers here, sometimes a policy written in another state entirely.

questions.q: How does Florida no-fault fit into a serious injury claim?

bullets.label: It pays first and it's small
bullets.detail: the coverage on your own policy handles the early bills and it runs out fast.

bullets.label: There's a fourteen-day clock
bullets.detail: see a doctor inside two weeks, or that coverage is gone entirely.

bullets.label: Serious injuries go outside it
bullets.detail: once an injury is permanent, the case moves past your own coverage and onto the policies behind whoever caused it.

bullets.label: Where that line sits
bullets.detail: the serious cases here are moved out of the county for treatment, so the proof that you crossed that line arrives from two hospitals rather than one.

questions.q: What extra protection exists when a truck causes the crash near Stuart?

bullets.label: The federal floor
bullets.detail: a carrier running interstate has to carry a minimum set by federal rule, well above any car policy.

bullets.label: A backstop behind it
bullets.detail: there's a federal guarantee that can force payment to an injured person even when the insurer says the policy doesn't cover it.

bullets.label: Where the trucks come from here
bullets.detail: the trucks through Martin County are mostly running the coast route, and there's a weigh station on I-95 that keeps inspection records on the ones that came through.

appendix_question_bank.question_text: When someone is seriously hurt in a commercial vehicle crash in Florida, why does the insurance behind the at-fault party matter so much?
What is a commercial insurance policy, and how is it different from the personal auto policy most people carry?
What are policy limits, and why are they the single most important number in a serious-injury case?
What kinds of commercial policies can be in play when a business vehicle or a truck causes a crash?
What does it actually mean to 'stack' coverage, and how do primary, excess, and umbrella layers fit together?
How does an umbrella policy work, and how is it different from an excess liability policy?
Can you stack insurance in Florida, and what does the law say about anti-stacking and the non-stacking election?
When the at-fault driver does not have enough coverage, how do uninsured and underinsured motorist coverage step in?
How does Florida PIP / No-Fault coverage fit in, and when does a serious injury let you step outside the No-Fault system?
In a trucking case, what is the MCS-90 endorsement and what does it actually cover for an injured person?
How much insurance are trucking companies required to carry under federal law, and how do those minimums shape a case?
What is bobtail or non-trucking-liability coverage, and why does it create coverage fights after a crash?
Beyond the driver, who else can be on the hook, and how does Florida's dangerous instrumentality doctrine pull in the vehicle owner?
How do negligent entrustment and broker or shipper liability open up additional policies in a trucking case?
What is a self-insured retention, and how is it different from a regular deductible when a big company is behind the crash?
What are captive insurers and fronting policies, and how can they hide or expose a defendant's real coverage?
How do lawyers actually find every insurance policy that might cover an accident?
Does an insurer in Florida have to disclose its policy limits, and what tools force that disclosure?
What does an insurer's duty to defend and duty to indemnify mean, and why does the difference matter to an injured person?
How do policy exclusions and a reservation-of-rights letter become the insurer's way of fighting coverage?
What is insurance bad faith, and how does Florida's bad-faith statute create real pressure to pay full value?
What is a policy-limits demand, and what is the Florida Civil Remedy Notice that has to come before a bad-faith suit?
What happens when the damages are worth more than every policy limit combined?
What is the single most important thing an injured Floridian should understand about commercial coverage and policy stacks?
